notes.b: Geographers describe where and why a settlement exists with three terms: site, situation and function. Keeping them apart lets you explain a settlement's location precisely.
points: Site is the exact ground a settlement is built on, such as a dry point (a patch of dry ground in wet land), a wet point (a water source), a defensive hill, a river loop, a bridging point (where a river can be crossed) or a sheltered harbour.
Example of site: Mount Sandel, near Coleraine, Co. Derry, on a bluff (a steep bank) above the River Bann.

Situation is where the settlement lies relative to the land around it, including its routes, resources and hinterland (the surrounding area it serves). Example: Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, beside the River Shannon where the Esker Riada routeway (a ridge of glacial gravel used as a road) crosses it.
Function is the economic and social purpose of a settlement, what people there do. Example: Glendalough, Co. Wicklow, where a monastery (a community of monks) served a religious function.
notes.tip: Define site, situation and function separately and give an Irish example for each, as exam answers on location use these terms.

notes.h: Locational factors common to all periods
notes.b: People in every period chose where to settle using the same practical factors. Later blocks apply these factors to each period in turn, and they are the reasons an exam answer on why a town developed at its location should give.
points: Water supply: a river, lake or spring gave drinking water, fishing and a means of transport.
Defence: high ground, cliffs, river loops, islands and marsh edges made a site harder to attack.
Fertile, well-drained land: soil that supported crops and grazing without flooding.
Shelter: sheltered valleys, bays and estuaries (wide river mouths where the river meets the sea) protected people and boats from the weather.
Routeways and fords or bridging points: places where roads, valleys or rivers could be crossed easily, so people and trade passed through.
Resources: fish, timber and stone, which were needed for food, fuel and building.
Religious or political importance: a holy site or a seat of power attracted people and the services they needed.
Finding and naming historic settlements on an OS map is a separate skill. There is more on this in Map interpretation.
notes.tip: When asked why a town developed where it did, use these reasons: bridging point, route focus, defence, river, coast or harbour, fertile hinterland, religious site.

notes.b: The Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) people were the first to live in Ireland. They were hunter-gatherers, meaning they lived by hunting, fishing and collecting wild food rather than farming, so they had no reason to stay in one place.
points: They made temporary camps on coasts, lakeshores and river banks, where they could fish and gather food. This is why their sites are camps, not farms.
Mount Sandel, near Coleraine, Co. Derry, is the earliest known house site in Ireland. It is Mesolithic and over 9,000 years old, such as a camp beside a river.
The people of Mount Sandel fished for salmon and eels and gathered hazelnuts, which shows how they lived off wild food.

notes.b: Neolithic (New Stone Age) farmers cleared forest for fields and lived in permanent farmsteads, so settlement became fixed in place. They left large stone tombs and field walls that still survive.
points: Megalithic tombs (tombs built of huge stones) were built on high, visible ground, so they could be seen across the landscape. The main types are court, portal (dolmen), passage and wedge tombs.
Poulnabrone, in the Burren, Co. Clare, is a portal tomb (dolmen), such as the Neolithic tombs built on high, visible ground.
Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath, lies in a bend of the River Boyne and holds the passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth.
Newgrange is about 5,000 years old (about 3200 BC). Brú na Bóinne has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place protected as important to all humanity) since 1993.
Céide Fields, near Ballycastle, north Co. Mayo, is a Neolithic field system of stone walls preserved under blanket bog (a thick layer of peat that grew over the land). It is over 5,000 years old.
The walls of the Céide Fields show organised farming in the Neolithic period, because the fields were planned and divided by walls.
notes.tip: Megalithic tombs are mainly Neolithic. Match them to the period, not to the Bronze Age or later.

notes.h: Bronze Age and Iron Age sites
notes.b: In the Bronze Age and Iron Age people learned to work metal, and defence and royal power began to shape where they settled. Some sites were for ceremony or kingship rather than everyday living.
points: Metalworking developed in the Bronze Age and Iron Age, so tools and weapons improved. Standing stones and stone circles survive from this period.
Fulachta fia were Bronze Age cooking sites beside streams, so water was close at hand.
Hillforts and promontory forts (forts on headlands jutting into the sea) gave defence on high ground and headlands.
Dún Aonghasa, on Inis Mór in the Aran Islands, Co. Galway, is a stone fort on the edge of a sheer sea cliff, so the cliff itself defends one side.
Crannógs were artificial islands in lakes, used over a long period. The water around them made them hard to attack.
The Hill of Tara, Co. Meath, was the traditional seat of the High Kings of Ireland. This is why it was a ceremonial site, not a town.
Navan Fort (Emain Macha), Co. Armagh, was the royal site of Ulster.
The Hill of Tara and Navan Fort were royal and ceremonial sites, not towns.
notes.tip: Fulachta fia are Bronze Age. Tara and Navan Fort are royal or ceremonial sites, not towns.

notes.b: From the 5th century, in the early Christian (early medieval) period, many farmers lived in defended farmsteads called ringforts. Unlike the later towns, these were spread across the countryside.
points: Ringforts (raths and lios; stone versions are cashels, cahers and dúns) were dispersed (spread out, not clustered), defended farmsteads, enclosed by a bank and ditch or a stone wall.
Ringforts were built on well-drained hillsides, which kept the farmstead dry and gave a view of approaching danger.
Souterrains were underground stone passages built alongside ringforts, so they are found at ringfort sites.
Over 40,000 ringforts survive in Ireland.
Place-name evidence: kil or cill (church), rath or lios (ringfort) and dun (fort) mark early Christian sites, so a townland name can show an old settlement.
Ringforts are early medieval. They are not prehistoric, Viking or Norman.
notes.tip: Ringforts are early Christian (early medieval) farmsteads. Do not call them Norman, Viking or prehistoric, and give no figure beyond over 40,000.

notes.b: Monasteries were the first centres of people and trade in the early Christian period. They were proto-towns (early forms of town), not true towns, because they lacked the full range of town functions.
points: Monasteries were sited on routeways, rivers, eskers (long ridges of glacial gravel that made dry routes) or remote islands, so they were either easy to reach or secluded.
Glendalough, Co. Wicklow, was founded by St Kevin in the 6th century in a glaciated valley (a valley shaped by ice).
Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, was founded by St Ciarán in the mid-6th century beside the River Shannon.
Skellig Michael, Co. Kerry, is an island monastery and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
Kells, Co. Meath, and Armagh are towns that grew from early monasteries.
Round towers served as bell towers and refuges, places to shelter from attack.
High crosses (tall carved stone crosses) and holy wells also mark early Christian sites.
notes.tip: Monasteries were proto-towns, not towns. Round towers and high crosses are early Christian features.

notes.h: Viking longphorts and the first towns
notes.b: The Vikings founded Ireland's first true towns, which began as fortified bases for their ships. They chose sites for trade and access by sea.
points: From the 9th century, Viking raids were followed by longphorts, fortified ship bases.
The Vikings sited their settlements on sheltered estuaries and harbours at river mouths, for trade and access by sea.
Dublin was founded as a longphort in 841, on the Liffey near its mouth, so ships could come and go by sea.
Waterford was founded by Vikings in 914, on the Suir estuary, so ships could reach the sea.
Limerick was a Viking settlement from about 922, on an island in the Shannon, which made it easy to defend.
Wexford and Cork were also Viking towns. Like Dublin, they were coastal or estuary sites suited to trade by sea.
Norse (Viking) place names include Wexford, Waterford, Wicklow and Arklow. Leixlip, Co. Kildare, comes from Old Norse for salmon leap.
Wood Quay, Dublin: excavations in the 1970s uncovered a large Viking town site. There is more on this in Urban problems in developed-world cities.
notes.tip: The Vikings founded Ireland's first towns. Do not say the Normans founded Dublin, Waterford or Limerick.

notes.b: The Normans (Anglo-Normans) took over and extended existing Viking towns rather than founding them. They also built castles to hold the land they conquered.
points: The Normans landed at Bannow Bay, Co. Wexford, in 1169.
Strongbow (Richard de Clare) took Waterford in 1170, a Viking town, which shows the Normans captured towns rather than founding them.
Motte and bailey castles came first. A motte was an earth mound topped by a wooden tower, with a fortified enclosure (the bailey) beside it. Stone castles followed.
Trim Castle, Co. Meath, on the River Boyne, is the largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland, a stone castle of the kind that followed the mottes. Hugh de Lacy began it in the 1170s.
Carrickfergus Castle, Co. Antrim, was built by John de Courcy from 1177.
notes.tip: Mottes and walled towns are Norman. The Normans captured and expanded Viking towns.

notes.h: Norman walled towns and manor villages
notes.b: Norman towns were sited at bridging points and on navigable rivers in fertile lowlands, for defence and control of land and trade. They were planned places with a set of recognisable features.
points: Walled towns had gates, market squares, charters (documents granting the town rights), burgage plots (long narrow strips of land rented by townspeople), parish churches and abbeys. The walls gave defence and the market square supported trade.
Manor villages grew up around a lord's manor (his estate and house), with tenants farming the surrounding land.
Athenry, Co. Galway, and Fethard, Co. Tipperary, have among the most complete medieval town walls in Ireland, which survive as evidence of Norman defence.
notes.tip: Athenry and Fethard have among the most complete town walls. Derry has the only complete city walls. Do not swap these.

notes.b: Kilkenny shows how a Norman town became a centre of power. Its castle, and later laws and assemblies, tie it to the history of Norman Ireland.
points: Kilkenny is a Norman town on the River Nore. A stone castle was built there by William Marshal around 1200.
The Statutes of Kilkenny, 1366, tried to stop the Normans adopting Irish language and customs.
The Confederation of Kilkenny was formed in 1642.

notes.b: After the first Norman phase, lords built fortified homes of their own. Outside the Norman towns, much of the country was run on a different pattern.
points: Tower houses were fortified homes of local lords, built in the 15th and 16th centuries, so lords could defend themselves.
Gaelic Ireland (the parts ruled by Irish lords, not the Normans) was largely without towns.

notes.b: A plantation was the official settling of land with new settlers loyal to the Crown. The Laois and Offaly, Munster and Ulster plantations each produced planned towns.
points: Plantation of Laois and Offaly, 1556: Maryborough (now Portlaoise) and Philipstown (now Daingean) were planned as plantation towns.
Munster Plantation, from the 1580s: Bandon, Co. Cork, is a plantation town.
Plantation towns had a central square or diamond, a wide main street, a market house and an Established (Protestant) church. Donegal town is an Ulster example.
Ulster Plantation, from 1609: Derry was renamed Londonderry in 1613.
Derry's city walls were built 1613–1618. They are the only complete city walls in Ireland.
notes.tip: Derry's walls are the only complete city walls in Ireland. Do not confuse them with Athenry and Fethard, which have among the most complete town walls.

notes.b: Improving landlords (estate owners who invested in their land) laid out planned towns beside their estates, with wide streets, squares, malls (tree-lined walks) and market houses. Georgian (18th-century) towns followed the same orderly pattern.
points: Westport, Co. Mayo, was laid out in the 18th century by the Browne family of Westport House. It has the Octagon and a tree-lined Mall along the Carrowbeg River.
Birr, Co. Offaly, is a Georgian planned town of the Parsons family (Earls of Rosse), built beside Birr Castle, so the landlord's home and his town sit together.
The Leviathan telescope at Birr, built in 1845, was the largest telescope in the world for decades.
Kenmare, Co. Kerry, was laid out in 1775 by the first Marquess of Lansdowne.
Adare, Co. Limerick, is an estate village of the Dunraven estate, with thatched cottages.
The Wide Streets Commissioners were set up in Dublin in 1757. Georgian Dublin has wide streets, squares such as Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square, and red-brick terraces (rows of joined houses).
Limerick's Georgian Newtown Pery was laid out in the late 18th century on land of Edmund Sexton Pery.
The full development of Georgian Dublin is a larger story. There is more on this in A Core Irish Region.

notes.h: Railways, workhouses and famine in the 19th century
notes.b: In the 19th century transport and industry created new towns, while poverty and famine emptied parts of the countryside.
points: Canals and railways created railway junction towns, where lines met and traffic changed, and seaside resorts, which people could now reach.
Mills and industrial villages were a feature of the 19th century.
The first railway in Ireland, Dublin–Kingstown (Dún Laoghaire), opened in 1834.
The Irish Poor Law Act of 1838 built a workhouse (an institution housing the poor) in each Poor Law union (a district grouped for poor relief).
The Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration emptied much of the rural west. This is why the west had fewer people afterwards.
Clonmel, Co. Tipperary: Charles Bianconi began Ireland's first public horse-drawn passenger car service there in 1815, so people could travel between towns.
Belfast grew on linen and shipbuilding, such as Harland and Wolff, who built the Titanic, launched in 1911.

notes.b: In the modern period the State began to plan new towns, and cities spread outward.
points: Shannon, Co. Clare, was Ireland's first planned new town. It was built from the 1960s for workers at the Shannon Free Zone (an area set up in 1959 to attract industry) beside Shannon Airport.
The Wright Report of 1967 set out new towns for Dublin at Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
Suburban expansion and commuter towns (towns whose residents travel out to work) grew outward from cities.

notes.h: Reading historic phases in a modern town: Kilkenny
notes.b: A modern Irish town keeps the features of each historic phase in its street pattern and buildings. Kilkenny is the worked example.
points: The street plan links Kilkenny Castle and the cathedral. It is promoted as the Medieval Mile. This is why the old castle and church still shape the town.
St Canice's Cathedral, with its round tower beside it, marks the early Christian monastery that gave the city its name, Cill Chainnigh, meaning church of Canice.
Kilkenny has city status.

In an Irish town, walls and gates date from the Norman period, the market square and market house from the plantation and landlord towns, Georgian terraces from the 18th century, and mills and the railway station from the 19th century.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to match a historic feature to its period. Higher Level asks for the historic development of an Irish town.

The position of a settlement relative to the routes, resources and surrounding land around it.
The economic and social purpose of a settlement.
A defended early Christian farmstead enclosed by a bank, known as a rath or lios; stone versions are cashels, cahers and dúns.
An underground stone passage built alongside a ringfort.
A settlement with some town functions, such as a monastery, that was not a true town.
A fortified Viking ship base, which became one of Ireland's first true towns.
Bronze Age cooking sites beside streams.
An artificial island in a lake, used over a long period.
An early Norman castle built on an earth mound with a fortified enclosure beside it.
A long, narrow plot of land in a Norman walled town.

A planned town with a central square or diamond, a wide main street, a market house and an Established church.

factCards.term: Locational factors that settlers used in every period
factCards.definition: Water supply; defence (hills, cliffs, river loops, islands); fertile, well-drained land; shelter in valleys, bays and estuaries; routeways, fords and bridging points; resources such as fish, timber and stone; religious or political importance.

factCards.term: Mount Sandel: location, age and how its people lived
factCards.definition: Near Coleraine, Co. Derry, on a bluff above the River Bann: the earliest known house site in Ireland, Mesolithic and over 9,000 years old. Its hunter-gatherers fished for salmon and eels and gathered hazelnuts.

factCards.term: Neolithic farmers: how settlement changed, with the Céide Fields
factCards.definition: Farmers cleared forest for fields and lived in permanent farmsteads; megalithic tombs stood on high, visible ground. Céide Fields, near Ballycastle, Co. Mayo: stone-walled fields under blanket bog, over 5,000 years old, evidence of organised farming.

factCards.term: Brú na Bóinne: location, tombs and two dates
factCards.definition: In a bend of the River Boyne, Co. Meath: the passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth. Newgrange is about 5,000 years old (about 3200 BC). A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

factCards.term: Bronze Age and Iron Age: settlement features and named sites
factCards.definition: Standing stones and stone circles; fulachta fia beside streams; hillforts and promontory forts, e.g. Dún Aonghasa, a stone fort on a sheer sea cliff on Inis Mór; crannógs; royal sites at Tara (High Kings) and Navan Fort (Ulster), not towns.

factCards.term: Ringforts: where they were built, how many survive, place-name clues
factCards.definition: Early Christian farmsteads, from the 5th century, dispersed on well-drained hillsides. Over 40,000 survive in Ireland. Place names with rath, lios or lis and dun mark ringforts; kil or cill marks a church.

factCards.term: Early Christian monasteries: where they were sited, three examples
factCards.definition: On routeways, rivers, eskers or remote islands: Glendalough (St Kevin, 6th century, glaciated valley); Clonmacnoise (St Ciarán, where the Esker Riada crosses the Shannon); Skellig Michael (island). Kells and Armagh grew into towns from monasteries.

factCards.term: Viking settlement: site factors and Norse place names
factCards.definition: From the 9th century, raids gave way to longphorts on sheltered estuaries and harbours at river mouths, for trade and access by sea; they became the first true towns. Norse names: Wexford, Waterford, Wicklow, Arklow, Leixlip (salmon leap).

factCards.term: Viking towns: three foundation dates and their sites
factCards.definition: Dublin, 841, on the Liffey near its mouth; Waterford, 914, on the Suir estuary; Limerick, from about 922, on an island in the Shannon. Wexford and Cork were also Viking towns.

factCards.term: Normans: arrival dates and two named castles
factCards.definition: Landed at Bannow Bay, Co. Wexford, 1169; Strongbow took Waterford, 1170. Motte and bailey first, then stone castles: Trim, on the Boyne, the largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland, begun by Hugh de Lacy in the 1170s; Carrickfergus, by John de Courcy from 1177.

factCards.term: Norman walled towns: site factors, features and two examples
factCards.definition: Sited at bridging points and on navigable rivers in fertile lowlands, for defence and control of land and trade. Walls and gates, market square, charter, burgage plots, parish church, abbeys. Athenry and Fethard: among the most complete town walls.

factCards.term: Norman Kilkenny: three facts with dates
factCards.definition: A Norman town on the River Nore, with a stone castle built by William Marshal around 1200; the Statutes of Kilkenny, 1366, tried to stop the Normans adopting Irish language and customs; the Confederation of Kilkenny was formed in 1642.

factCards.term: Kilkenny today: how its historic phases show in the city
factCards.definition: St Canice's Cathedral and its round tower mark the early Christian monastery that named the city, Cill Chainnigh (church of Canice); Kilkenny Castle and the Norman core on the Nore; the street plan linking castle and cathedral is the Medieval Mile.

factCards.term: Plantation towns: three plantations with a named town from each
factCards.definition: Laois and Offaly, 1556: Maryborough (Portlaoise), Philipstown (Daingean). Munster, from the 1580s: Bandon. Ulster, from 1609: Donegal town around a diamond; Derry, renamed Londonderry in 1613, whose walls (1613–1618) are Ireland's only complete city walls.

factCards.term: Name three 18th-century landlord towns and who laid them out
factCards.definition: Westport, Co. Mayo: Browne family of Westport House; the Octagon and a tree-lined Mall on the Carrowbeg River. Birr, Co. Offaly: Parsons family (Earls of Rosse), beside Birr Castle. Kenmare, Co. Kerry: first Marquess of Lansdowne, 1775.

factCards.term: Georgian Dublin and Limerick: who shaped them and when
factCards.definition: Dublin's Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and laid out the city's streets; Georgian Dublin also has squares such as Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square, and red-brick terraces. Limerick's Newtown Pery was laid out in the late 18th century on land of Edmund Sexton Pery.

Canals and railways created junction towns and resorts (first railway, Dublin–Kingstown, 1834); the 1838 Poor Law Act built a workhouse in each union; the Famine (1845–49) and emigration emptied much of the rural west; Belfast grew on linen and shipbuilding.

factCards.term: 20th-century planned settlement: Shannon and Dublin's new towns
factCards.definition: Shannon, Co. Clare: Ireland's first planned new town, built from the 1960s for workers at the Shannon Free Zone (set up 1959) beside Shannon Airport. The Wright Report, 1967, planned new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.

factCards.term: Modern Irish town: which period each historic feature dates from
factCards.definition: Round tower and church on a monastic site: early Christian; walls, gates and castle: Norman; central square or diamond and market house: plantation and landlord towns; Georgian terraces: 18th century; mills and railway station: 19th century.

questions.prompt: Examine the locational characteristics of pre-historic and historic settlements in Ireland, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Neolithic farmers settled on fertile, well-drained land and built megalithic tombs on high, visible ground. Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath, lies in a bend of the River Boyne, and Céide Fields, near Ballycastle, Co. Mayo, show organised farming. Early Christian settlement: ringforts were dispersed, defended farmsteads on well-drained hillsides, and over 40,000 survive. Monasteries were sited on routeways, rivers, eskers or remote islands: Clonmacnoise lies beside the Shannon where the Esker Riada crosses it, and Glendalough lies in a glaciated valley. Viking settlement: longphorts were placed on sheltered estuaries and harbours at river mouths for trade and access by sea, as at Dublin, founded in 841 on the Liffey near its mouth, and Waterford, founded in 914 on the Suir estuary. Norman settlement: towns were sited at bridging points and on navigable rivers in fertile lowlands, for defence and control of land and trade. Trim Castle, on the River Boyne, was begun by Hugh de Lacy in the 1170s, and Athenry has among the most complete medieval town walls in Ireland.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the historic development of one Irish town you have studied.
questions.model: Kilkenny began with an early Christian monastery, St Canice's, whose name Cill Chainnigh means church of Canice. Its round tower stands beside the cathedral. The Normans built a town on the River Nore with a stone castle, built by William Marshal around 1200. The Statutes of Kilkenny, 1366, tried to stop the Normans adopting Irish language and customs. The Confederation of Kilkenny was formed in 1642. The medieval street plan that links the castle and the cathedral survives today as the Medieval Mile, and Kilkenny has city status.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Vikings and the Normans chose the sites they did for their settlements in Ireland.
questions.model: Vikings: they chose sheltered estuaries and harbours at river mouths, for trade and access by sea. Dublin was founded in 841 on the Liffey near its mouth. Waterford was founded in 914 on the Suir estuary. Their longphorts were fortified ship bases. Normans: they chose bridging points and navigable rivers in fertile lowlands, for defence and control of land and trade. Trim Castle, on the River Boyne, is the largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland. Their towns had walls, gates and market squares, which gave protection and a centre for trade.
